title: Should you still write code?
text:
For statistical analysis and data-science projects, lately I’ve been contemplating the question of whether we should still write code given the power of modern AI tools like Claude Code/Codex that can easily write code for us. Specifically, I’ve been thinking about several options:
I’m still trying to form my thoughts and beliefs on this topic, but in the meantime I want to share some resources I’ve found helpful while exploring these questions.

title: Should you still write code?
section: 1.1 Growth requires friction and AI removes it
text:
1.1 Growth requires friction and AI removes it
He recently gave an excellent talk at the 2026 R+AI conference called Friction Worth Keeping: What Keeps Us Human When AI Makes Everything Easy.
The introduction of the article provides a nice summary:

Generative AI removes friction. Need a poster for an event? Slides for stakeholders? An R package to access an API? An answer for a problem set? A feature requiring major refactoring? It’s all a prompt away. Incidental, frustrating friction is disappearing.


But not all friction is bad. Some friction is formative and central to the human experience. Struggling to learn develops skills and expertise. Creating things slowly gives us time to reflect and develop taste. Working through hard problems builds understanding and judgment. Contributing to a community builds trust.


AI can eliminate all kinds of friction, producing output that looks polished and convincing whether it’s grounded in human understanding or hollow underneath. How can we tell what friction is worth keeping? This talk explores the difference between friction that gets in our way and friction that makes us who we are, and what keeps us human when our work becomes effortless.

It’s harder to tell if a given product/output is trustworthy now:

I think this is one of the most dangerous features of AI: it trashes our existing heuristics for effort and trust. It used to be that making a slick video or writing a 40-page document implied that you cared enough to at least put in the effort, but now those signals are gone. It’s becoming increasingly difficult to tell what work represents genuine human effort and caring, and what work is the result of a few minutes of prompting and a few dollars of token spend. - Hadley Wickham

He also shared a nice forklift/weightlifting analogy that has been circulating online:

Using ChatGPT to complete assignments is like bringing a forklift into the weight room; you will never improve your cognitive fitness that way. - Ted Chiang

title: Should you still write code?
section: 1.2 Using AI to teach and help you how to code
text:
1.2 Using AI to teach and help you how to code
Andrew often emphasizes that AIs can be used to teach, explain and help you write code, rather than do all coding for you with little to no human involvement.
Some relevant quotes from this article:

Instead of asking “What’s the average of this column” and getting some made up number, you can ask “How can I calculate the average of this column” and get code like mean(dataset$column), which you can then inspect yourself and make sure it makes sense and is the right thing to use.


they help you create the code necessary for analyzing data. This, I think, is the future of LLMs/AI in data analysis. It still has to be human driven, with humans making decisions and humans looking at the code and humans understanding the code and humans running the code and humans writing about the output.

title: Should you still write code?
text:
1.3 Rules for using AI
Here are some of Andrew’s tips for how he uses AI, I find these interesting and plan to try them out:

To avoid falling into over-reliance on LLM-assisted code help, I add as much friction into my workflow as possible. I only use GitHub Copilot and Claude in the browser, not through the chat sidebar in Positron or Visual Studio Code. When I use Claude Code, I don’t use it in real projects—I use it in separate projects with simulated data and have it create Quarto files explaining what it does. I treat the code LLMs generate like random answers from StackOverflow or blog posts and generally rewrite it completely. I disable the inline LLM-based auto complete in text editors…

I’ve been using the Claude Code extension in Positron for a while now but I’m tempted to try switching back to the online browser version as Andrew recommends. Or at a minimum, if I do use Claude Code in Positron, trying to use it more in separate environments with simulated data rather than the actual project data.

title: Should you still write code?
section: 2.1 You need to write, read and understand your code
text:
2.1 You need to write, read and understand your code
Carson often refers to The Sorcerer’s Apprentice Trap scene in the Disney movie Fantasia to explain why it’s so important for us to read and understand our code, and to prevent unnecessary complexity that can easily get out of control:

“…Yes, AI can generate the code for this assignment. Don’t let it. You have to write the code.”
I explain that, if they don’t write the code, they will not be able to effectively read the code. The ability to read code is certainly going to be valuable, maybe more valuable, in an AI-based coding future.
If you can’t read the code you are going to fall into The Sorcerer’s Apprentice Trap, creating systems you don’t understand and can’t control.
…LLM generated code, on the other hand, often does not eliminate accidental complexity and, in fact, can add significant accidental complexity by choosing inappropriate approaches to problems, taking shortcuts, etc.
If you can’t read the code, how can you tell? And if you want to read the code you must write the code. - Carson Gross

As he explains in another article:

One movie scene that has been consistently coming back to me as I have watched AI garner more and more attention is The Sorcerer’s Apprentice from Disney’s movie Fantasia.
In this scene the apprentice decides to use magic to assist in the drudgery of cleaning. He enchants a broom which then proceeds to start cleaning things up. Things appear to be going swimmingly for a while, until the broom starts cleaning more and more vigorously, reaching a point where things start going swimmingly literally.
The chaos is resolved when the Sorcerer reappears and asserts control over the situation, glaring at the apprentice for his foolishness.
This seems like an apt metaphor for the AI era: you want to be a sorcerer and not an apprentice.
And a sorcerer has to understand the code. - Carson Gross

Similar to Andrew, Carson also recommends using AI as a teacher and helper when writing code, rather than using AI to write all of the code for you:

Another thing that I tell my students is that AI, used properly, is a tremendously effective TA. If you don’t use it as a code-generator but rather as a partner to help you understand concepts and techniques, it can provide a huge boost to your intellectual development.
One of the most difficult things when learning computer programming is getting “stuck”. You just don’t see the trick or know where to even start well enough to make progress.
AI can help you get past these roadblocks, and can be a great TA if used correctly

title: Introduction to survival (time-to-event) analysis
text:
1 Intro

Quick intro
Example R code for common survival analysis methods. Covers 3 of the most common methods used in survival analysis: log-rank test and Kaplan Meir plots for comparing survival curves between groups, and Cox proportional hazards regression model.
logrank test for comparing survival curves between groups



2 How to interpret hazard ratios

https://journals.asm.org/doi/full/10.1128/aac.48.8.2787-2792.2004
The “hazard ratio” is the most common effect size used in survival analysis. Briefly, it compares the risk of having the event occur in the next instant between groups



3 Regression for time-to-event outcomes

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-022-01689-8
Intro to the Cox proportional hazard model (most common regression model for survival data)
Also introduces the accelerated failure time model (AFTR). Although less commonly used , this model has a nice interpretation that uses “time ratios”: it compares the ratio of the average time of event in group 1 to the average time of event in group 2.



4 Machine learning
Here are 2 popular machine learning models used for time-to-event outcomes:

Regularized Cox model (i.e. a modified version of the Cox model that performs automatic feature selection)
Random survival forest. Perhaps you’ve heard of “random forests” before, it is one of the most popular machine learning methods that has been shown to work well across a wide variety of applications.

The C-index can be used to assess the predictive accuracy of a survival model. It is similar to the AUROC in that it ranges from 0 to 1, with 0.5 indicating no predictive ability and 1 indicating perfect predictive ability. Most survival model R functions will calculate the C-index for you, but if not, there are a few R packages for calculating it and comparing C between different models: survcomp, compareC, survC1

title: Imputing missing data
text:
Missing data analysis: Making it work in the real world

Multiple imputation is the gold standard method for handling missing data but is computationally intensive.
EM algorithm works well, but lack of general software.
If doing likelihood-based regression modeling, then as long as you adjust for variables that influence missingness, results will not be biased due to missing data (although patients with missing values are dropped from the model, thus decreasing power).

Imputation likely still better due to improved power (i.e. all patients can be included).

title: Imputing missing data
text:
2.1 Continuous

set.seed(123)

data('geno', package = 'missMDA')

# impute.knn (features in rows, samples in cols)
# this is my preferred method for high dimensional continuous data since it is relatively fast
knn.imp <- impute::impute.knn(t(geno))$data
knn.imp <- data.frame(t(knn.imp), check.names = FALSE)

# PCA (samples in rows, features in cols)
ncomp <- missMDA::estim_ncpPCA(geno, ncp.min = 0, ncp.max = 6)
pca.imp <- missMDA::imputePCA(geno, ncp = ncomp$ncp, scale = TRUE)$completeObs

# missForest
mf.imp <- missForest::missForest(geno)$ximp

title: Imputing missing data
text:
2.2 Categorical

data('vnf', package = 'missMDA')

# missForest
mf.imp <- missForest::missForest(vnf)$ximp

# MCA
#ncomp <- missMDA::estim_ncpMCA(vnf); # slow method to estimate number of components
mca.imp <- missMDA::imputeMCA(vnf, ncp = 3)$complete.obs

title: Imputing missing data
text:
2.3 Mixed continuous/categorical

data('snorena', package = 'missMDA')

# missForest
mf.imp <- missForest::missForest(snorena)$ximp

# FAMD
#missMDA::estim_ncpFAMD(snorena); # slow method to estimate number of components
famd.imp <- missMDA::imputeFAMD(snorena, ncp = 3)$completeObs
